title: Perfect hash join for RIGHT joins with dense keys up to 2^22
hypothesis: q13 HASH_JOIN (RIGHT, o_custkey = c_custkey, build = 1.5M customer keys, dense) costs 1.76s CPU of the ~2.5s query. PerfectHashJoinExecutor::CanDoPerfectHashJoin (perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp:73) rejects every join type except INNER, and MAX_BUILD_SIZE=1048576 (line 108) is below a 1.5M key range. Two more gates also block it: JoinFilterPushdownOptimizer's compute_aggregates_anyway (join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp:275) is INNER-only, so with the probe key behind a compress projection there is no build min/max; and the dup check `ht.Count() > build_range` (line 115) is off by one (the range holds build_range+1 values), so it rejects every fully dense key set, INNER joins included. In an earlier run of this system the same change took the join from 1.87s to 0.19s CPU (q13 -20%).
plan: 1) perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp CanDoPerfectHashJoin: also allow JoinType::RIGHT (and the matching RIGHT_SEMI/ANTI only if simple), raise MAX_BUILD_SIZE to 1<<22, fix the dup check to `ht.Count() > build_range + 1`. 2) In the perfect build fill (FullScanHashTable/BuildPerfectHashTable), check build-key validity, because RIGHT joins keep NULL-key build rows with has_null=false. For RIGHT joins, set the found-match flag in the HT row (the same flag the normal HT uses for the RIGHT outer scan) when probing, so that PhysicalHashJoin's existing ScanFullOuter still emits unmatched build rows. Or, simpler, keep a per-slot bool matched array and change the outer scan. Pick whichever the existing code supports with less change. 3) join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp:275: set compute_aggregates_anyway for RIGHT joins too, so build min/max gets computed. 4) Check that physical_hash_join.cpp:1004 then takes the perfect path. Add a sqllogictest for RIGHT/LEFT join with NULL build keys, duplicate keys, and unmatched rows.
generality: Any LEFT/RIGHT outer join where a dense integer key is built (FK->PK outer joins, common in TPC-H/DS style queries). INNER joins with a fully dense key range also gain from the off-by-one fix. Downside: memory for ranges up to 4M slots, so keep a density guard (count >= range/4 or similar).
risk: Medium: outer-join correctness (unmatched build rows, NULL keys, duplicate build keys must fall back). The previous run hit 3 silent gates; check each one with EXPLAIN ANALYZE/profile.

title: SIMD first+last-byte candidate filter in FindStrInStr with overlapping tail block
hypothesis: q13 orders TABLE_SCAN with the `o_comment NOT LIKE '%a%b%'` filter takes 2.58s CPU, the largest operator. like.cpp:260/285 calls FindStrInStr (contains.cpp:76), which uses memchr on the first needle byte and then memcmp; on ~50-byte comments with common first bytes this means many memchr calls/branches. An SSE2/SWAR scan comparing the first and last needle bytes at their offsets over 16-byte blocks filters candidates in bulk. In the previous run a scalar tail killed the gain (-2%), while an overlapping final block gave q13 -12%.
plan: contains.cpp FindStrInStr(const unsigned char*,...): for needle_size>=2 and haystack_size <= 256, loop over 16-byte blocks: load hay[i..i+16] and hay[i+n-1..i+n-1+16], cmpeq against the broadcast first/last byte, AND, movemask; for each set bit, memcmp the middle. For the final partial block, load an overlapping block ending at the last valid start and shift the mask to drop positions already checked; no scalar tail. Guard with __SSE2__, otherwise use a 64-bit SWAR fallback or the existing path. Keep the existing path for long haystacks.
generality: All contains/LIKE '%x%'/strpos/string_split on short strings, which are common in analytical filters. Long strings are unchanged.
risk: Low-medium: off-by-one in the overlap mask and reads past the end of the buffer (only load inside [0, haystack_size)). Fuzz with sqllogictests for needles at the start/end and haystacks of 1..40 bytes.

title: Large perfect hash aggregate (up to 22 bits) with parallel combine and source
hypothesis: q13 inner HASH_GROUP_BY on c_custkey (1.5M groups, dense integer key, count) costs 2.51s CPU. The radix HT is used because the key range exceeds perfect_ht_threshold. A perfect array aggregate indexed by key-min avoids hashing/probing. The earlier run measured -18.6%, but only after the combine (striped locks) and the source (block-parallel scan) were parallelised; serial versions gave 3.6%.
plan: physical_perfect_hash_aggregate / the planner selection in plan_aggregate.cpp: allow perfect HA when stats give a range up to 2^22 with a density/memory guard; make Combine merge in parallel over stripes, and make GetData a parallel source over blocks of slots.
generality: GROUP BY on dense integer keys (PKs/FKs) with large cardinality. Sparse ranges stay on radix because of the density guard.
risk: Medium-high: larger diff; per-thread memory of 4M slots x threads, so it needs a memory guard.

title: Vector-at-once substring prefilter for LIKE/contains scan filters on FSST columns
hypothesis: After E0001 and E0003, the orders TABLE_SCAN with the pushed `o_comment NOT LIKE '%a%b%'` ExpressionFilter takes 2.54s of about 3.6s total CPU in q13 (profile.md). Standalone timings split that cost: `sum(length(o_comment))` (FSST decode only) runs in about 106 ms. The same scan with `NOT LIKE '%x%y%'` takes 236 ms, `contains(col,'x')` 215 ms, and a suffix-only `LIKE '%zzzz'` 110 ms. So about half the scan is the per-row substring search: LikeMatcher::Match (like.cpp:231) calls FindStrInStr for each row (contains.cpp:76), which is a memchr on the needle's first byte followed by a Load/compare loop. With 48-byte strings and a common first letter, that means several memchr calls and branch mispredictions per row across 15M rows. FSST has no compression->filter, so StandardColumnData::Filter falls back to ColumnData::Filter (column_data.cpp:348). That function scans an FSST_VECTOR, flattens it with ToUnifiedFormat (each string decoded separately into the heap), then evaluates the expression row by row through ColumnSegment::FilterSelection's EXPRESSION_FILTER case (column_segment.cpp:563). If the vector's strings are decoded into one contiguous buffer and the required literal is searched once over the whole buffer (about 100KB per vector), the search costs a few ns per row instead of tens. Rows with no occurrence get their LIKE result without any per-row work.
plan: In ColumnData::Filter (src/storage/table/column_data.cpp:348), before ToUnifiedFormat, add a fast path. It applies when: (a) after Scan the result is VectorType::FSST_VECTOR; (b) the filter is an ExpressionFilter whose expr is exactly a BoundFunctionExpression `~~` (LIKE), `!~~` (NOT LIKE) or `contains`, with child 0 a BoundReferenceExpression and child 1 a constant VARCHAR without collation, optionally wrapped once in NOT. For LIKE the pattern must contain no '_' and no escape, and must have at least one literal segment of at least 2 bytes between % signs or at the start/end (reuse the segment-splitting logic of LikeMatcher::CreateLikeMatcher in like.cpp:290; copy it or expose a small static helper that returns the longest literal segment). Then: 1) Decode all scan_count strings into ONE contiguous buffer allocated from the result vector's string heap, so its lifetime matches the vector. Get the decoder from FSSTVector::GetDecoder and the compressed string_t values from FSSTVector::GetCompressedData<string_t>. Bound the buffer size by the compressed sizes × 8, the FSST max expansion, or by the sum of the decoded sizes. Decode each row with duckdb_fsst_decompress, the same call FSSTPrimitives::DecompressValue makes, into a running offset, record offsets[i], and write result_data[i] = string_t(ptr, len) so the result becomes a valid FLAT_VECTOR. Keep the FSST validity: NULL rows get an empty string and stay invalid. 2) Search for the needle across the whole buffer once. Use a SIMD candidate filter on the needle's first and last bytes (SSE2 16B, or AVX2 if available; E0002's code has an overlapping-tail version), memcmp the middle, and do not let a candidate start in the last needle_size-1 bytes of the buffer. Map each hit to its row by advancing a monotone row cursor over offsets, and accept it only if hit+needle_size <= row_end, so hits spanning two rows are rejected. After the first hit in a row, jump to that row's end. 3) Rows with no hit and a valid value: for LIKE or contains the result is false; for NOT LIKE it is true. Rows with a hit are candidates: evaluate the original expression on them only, by slicing the flat result with a candidate SelectionVector and reusing the existing EXPRESSION_FILTER logic (the ExpressionFilterState executor in ColumnSegment::FilterSelection), or by calling FilterSelection with an initial sel holding only the candidates. Merge the decided rows and the approved candidates into `sel` in ascending order and set s_count. NULL rows are never approved. Respect an incoming sel/approved count by only considering rows already in sel. In every other case, including flat vectors, non-matching expressions and AND/OR filters, keep the existing path unchanged. Optional, only if easy: when the compressed strings of consecutive rows are adjacent in the dictionary (stored in reverse order), decode them with a single duckdb_fsst_decompress call.
generality: Any substring-type filter pushed into a table scan over an FSST-compressed VARCHAR column: LIKE '%x%', NOT LIKE '%x%y%', contains(), and multi-segment LIKE. Common in analytical workloads such as TPC-H q9 (part names), q13 and q16 (comments). Prefix/suffix-only LIKE also gets cheaper decoding. Nothing should get slower: patterns that don't qualify, flat vectors and other compressions keep the old path. The worst case is a needle present in almost every row, where all rows fall through to the old per-row evaluation after an extra buffer search (≤ ~10% overhead on that filter).
risk: Medium. Risks are correctness at row boundaries (cross-row hits, empty strings, NULLs, strings ≤12 bytes that must be inlined in string_t), buffer sizing (strings over the block limit), and keeping sel order. The fast path must be verified against the old path with SQL: compare `col LIKE p` against `(col || '') LIKE p`, which disables pushdown, over a grid of patterns, including the needle at the start and end of a row, a needle spanning two adjacent rows, NOT LIKE with NULLs, and contains(). Also check with EXPLAIN that the filter is still pushed into the scan.

title: Fold compress(decompress(x)) pairs in compressed materialization
hypothesis: In the q13 plan the RIGHT HASH_JOIN output (15.3M rows) goes into a PROJECTION `#0, __internal_decompress_integral_bigint(#1, 1)` that costs 0.18s CPU. The next PROJECTION immediately re-compresses the same column with `__internal_compress_integral_uinteger(#1, 1)` (0.01s) for the PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY. That is about 5% of the query's ~3.5s CPU spent turning a uinteger with offset 1 into a bigint and back. CompressedMaterialization creates the compress projection for the aggregate without checking whether its input is the output of a decompress projection that the CM pass for the join created just below it. Both expressions are pure, and compress(decompress(x, m), m) with the same compressed type and offset is the identity on x, so the pair can be removed.
plan:
In src/optimizer/compressed_materialization.cpp, CompressedMaterialization::CreateCompressProjection (or TryCompressChild, before the compress expression is built for a binding):
1. If child_op is a LogicalProjection, check the expression that produces the binding being compressed. If it is a BoundFunctionExpression for an __internal_decompress_integral_* function whose argument is a BoundColumnRef of type T_c with offset constant m, and the new compress expression is __internal_compress_integral_<T_c> with the same constant m (compare the bound function names and constant Values), apply the fold.
2. The fold: replace the child projection's expression at that index with the decompress argument (type T_c), and make the new compress projection emit a plain BoundColumnRef of type T_c for that column. Keep the stats from the compress expression, because the range is the same.
3. Only fold when the binding is referenced only by the new compress projection. That holds in the tree because the child projection's only parent is the operator being compressed. Assert it, and give up the fold if the decompressed binding is used anywhere else, for example in other expressions of the materializing op such as join conditions.
Strings (__internal_decompress_string / compress_string) can follow the same pattern but are optional; do integral first.
Check with EXPLAIN on q13: the decompress_integral_bigint projection between HASH_JOIN and PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY should be gone, or reduced to plain column refs.
Verify the function names in src/function/scalar/compressed_materialization/ (compress_integral.cpp) before matching on them.
expected_gain: q13: about 0.19s of ~3.5s CPU, roughly -4..-6% wall.
generality: Any plan where a compressed-materialization join feeds an aggregate, distinct or order on the same column, which is common in TPC-H style join→group-by queries. It only removes work and never adds any. Nothing should get slower, except in the rare case where the compressed value now flows into the aggregate through a narrower path, which is still the same data.
risk: Low to medium. Getting the bindings or types wrong after replacing the expression could give wrong results or binder assertions. The fold must not fire when the offsets or compressed types differ, for example when the stats were updated between the two CM steps.

title: Batched per-vector FSST decode into one contiguous buffer
hypothesis: The orders scan is 2.5s of ~3.5s CPU in q13. Measured standalone: `count(*) WHERE length(o_comment)>3` costs 1.36s CPU for 15M rows (about 90ns per ~48B string), so most of the scan is FSST decode. FSSTScanState::DecompressString (fsst.cpp:556) does several things for every row: str_len==0 and all_values_inlined branches, AllocateShrinkableBuffer(len*8) with an arena Allocate call, duckdb_fsst_decompress with a per-string 32-byte slack check and a branchy tail, and then FinalizeShrinkableBuffer/ShrinkHead. Decoding a whole vector's strings back to back into one allocation would cut the allocator calls and keep the fast 4-code loop active for longer.
plan:
In FSSTStorage::StringScanPartial (src/storage/compression/fsst.cpp, the non-FSST-vector branch), when !all_values_inlined:
1. Sum the bitunpacked compressed lengths for the vector to get an upper bound of sum(len*8)+32.
2. Allocate once from StringVector::GetStringBuffer(result).
3. Call duckdb_fsst_decompress for each string into the running position, building string_t from the position and the decoded length. Strings of 12 bytes or less must be built as inlined string_t.
4. Shrink the unused tail once at the end.
Keep the existing path for the all_values_inlined and str_len==0 cases.
expected_gain: q13: uncertain, likely -3..-10%. Memory fsst-heap-reuse-no-gain warns that allocation may not be the bottleneck.
generality: Every scan of an FSST-compressed VARCHAR column. Some memory is held per vector until the shrink, but nothing should get slower.
risk: Low to medium. The decoder overwrites up to 8 bytes past each string, which needs slack at the end of the buffer. A wrong bound check would cause memory corruption.

title: COUNT-only perfect HA without per-thread tables for large ranges
hypothesis: Standalone `GROUP BY o_custkey count(o_orderkey)` on 15M rows: the PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY uses 0.28s CPU with 1 thread but 0.49-0.83s with 8 threads. Per-thread tables of 2^21 slots, the combine over 8x2M slots, and cache thrash are the overhead. In q13 the HA costs 0.49s CPU.
plan: For count/count_star-only aggregates with at least 2^16 slots, use thread-local plain int64 count arrays: no row layout and no group_is_set byte array, because count>0 can mark set slots for count_star but not for count(x). Combine with a SIMD add over stripes. Alternative: a single shared array with relaxed atomics, but cache-line ping-pong is a real risk, so measure it first.
generality: GROUP BY dense integer key with count aggregates. Skewed keys could suffer under the atomic variant.

title: Batched per-vector FSST decode with a shared output bound
hypothesis: The orders scan is 2.47s of ~3.5s CPU in q13, and measurements show FSST decode (~90ns per ~48B string) is most of it. Per row, FSSTScanState::DecompressString (fsst.cpp:556) calls FSSTPrimitives::DecompressValue (fsst.hpp:36). That does an arena Allocate(len*8), then duckdb_fsst_decompress with size=len*8, then FinalizeShrinkableBuffer/ShrinkHead. In duckdb_fsst_decompress (third_party/fsst/fsst.h:177) the fast 4-code loop only runs while posOut+32 <= size. Because size is only len*8, the last ~4 compressed bytes of every string fall into the branchy tail code, and strings shorter than 4 compressed bytes skip the fast loop completely. If the strings are decoded back to back into one per-vector allocation and size is passed as the remaining space in that allocation, the fast loop stays active up to each string's end. That also removes the per-row Allocate/ShrinkHead calls and the inline branches.
plan:
In FSSTStorage::StringScanPartial (src/storage/compression/fsst.cpp, the `else` branch around line 697, used when !all_values_inlined && decoder != nullptr) and in FSSTStorage::Select (line 724):
1. Sum the bit-unpacked compressed lengths bitunpack_buffer[offsets.scan_offset+i] over the rows to be decoded, giving total_bound = sum(len*8) + 32 slack.
2. Get one buffer with str_buffer.AllocateShrinkableBuffer(total_bound).
3. Keep a write position pos. For each row: if len==0, emit an empty string_t. Otherwise call n = duckdb_fsst_decompress(decoder, len, ptr, total_bound - pos, base+pos). If n <= string_t::INLINE_LENGTH, emit string_t(ptr, n), which copies the bytes inline, and do not advance pos. Otherwise emit string_t(base+pos, n) and advance pos += n.
4. At the end call allocator ShrinkHead(total_bound - pos), via a small new VectorStringBuffer helper next to FinalizeShrinkableBuffer in src/include/duckdb/common/types/vector_buffer.hpp. Before shrinking, construct every non-inlined string_t (the prefix is computed in the constructor) so that no later write touches the reclaimed tail. The decoder writes at most 8 bytes past each symbol, so the +32 slack covers it.
Keep the all_values_inlined path and the FSST-vector path unchanged. Check with SELECT count(*), sum(length(o_comment)), and also by comparing md5 of string_agg over a sample, that results match the old path.
expected_gain: q13: -4..-10%, from decode CPU (~1.4s of the scan) falling 10-25%.
generality: Every scan or select of a non-inlined FSST VARCHAR column: string filters, string group keys, and string output. Memory use per vector is the same, because shrinking happens once. Nothing should get slower, except slightly larger transient arena use within one vector.
risk: Low-medium. Memory-safety needs care: the bound must cover len*8 per string plus the 8-byte overwrite, with slack at the end; ShrinkHead must come after all writes. Inlined strings must be copied before pos is reused, which string_t(ptr,n) does.
